item.title: Multimodal neuroimaging fusion with interpretable deep learning for speech motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
PLOS digital health
Speech motor dysfunction affects approximately 90% of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), but multimodal neuroimaging models for prediction of this impairment remain limited. We developed MCTA-FusNet, an interpretable deep learning framework that integrates structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion MRI to predict speech motor dysfunction in PD. The model incorporates modality-specific encoders and a hierarchical triple-attention fusion mechanism to capture channel-, spatial-, and modality-level interactions. Using cross-domain transfer learning, MCTA-FusNet was first pretrained on the PPMI dataset (n = 400) to predict motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) and then fine-tuned on the FAH-SYSU dataset (n = 81) to predict speech motor dysfunction, indexed by vocal response magnitude (VRMag) to pitch perturbations. MCTA-FusNet outperformed all unimodal and multimodal models with transfer learning, achieving the lowest mean absolute error (1.388 ± 0.62) and highest correlation between predicted and observed VRMag (r = 0.731, p < 0.001). Interpretability analyses identified the superior temporal gyrus, primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, and supplementary motor area as key predictors, with greater coherence and phase synchrony between auditory and premotor regions significantly correlated with exaggerated VRMag. These findings establish a multimodal neuroimaging deep learning model for predicting and explaining speech motor dysfunction in PD, offering a novel framework with potential for symptom-specific monitoring and therapeutic intervention.

item.title: Predictors of Recovery From Aphasia After Stroke.
item.description:
Stroke
Predicting recovery from aphasia after stroke is challenging, yet essential. Accurate prognoses would enable stroke survivors and families to establish realistic expectations and make informed decisions, allow clinicians to plan rehabilitation, and inform the development and implementation of interventions. This review synthesizes current evidence on predictors of aphasia recovery, integrating diverse biological, behavioral, environmental, and temporal determinants into a unified conceptual framework organized around 3 fundamental determinants: the integrity of the language network, neuroplasticity throughout the remaining brain, and the passage of time. Lesion location and extent are powerful predictors, accounting for more than half of the variance in aphasia outcomes, but other interacting factors contribute to heterogeneous recovery trajectories, including variability in language network organization and effects of diaschisis. The capacity for neuroplasticity depends on the brain health and functionality of surviving tissue, but the realization of this potential depends critically on engagement in language use, which can be promoted by intensive speech-language therapy, social participation and supportive communication environments. Recovery follows a predictable decelerating time course, with rapid early gains driven primarily by reperfusion and resolution of dysfunction in brain regions that support language, and modest but meaningful longer-term improvements deriving from neuroplastic changes. This framework provides a practical heuristic for understanding aphasia recovery, developing clinical prediction tools, and identifying modifiable factors to optimize outcomes.

item.title: Hyperactivity of the posterior cingulate cortex during interpreting communicative intentions based on the speaker-listener relationship in autism spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Social neuroscience
Speakers' intended meanings are often inferred from extra-linguistic social factors such as the speaker-listener relationship, yet how individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) incorporate such relational cues remains unclear. Using fMRI, we investigated whether and how individuals with autism utilize speaker-listener relationship cues to interpret communicative intentions. Twenty adults with ASD and 20 matched typically developed (TD) controls completed a discourse comprehension task where the interpretation of a target remark depended on the speaker-listener relationship or not. Behaviorally, both groups showed faster reactions in the social factor condition, indicating that the social context facilitated their responses. However, the ASD group was less accurate overall. Across the groups, core discourse regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus, were engaged. Critically, ASD participants exhibited increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), whereas TD participants showed PCC deactivation. Functional connectivity analyses further indicated reduced PCC connectivity with the left angular gyrus and right fusiform gyrus in ASD compared with TD. These findings suggest that, despite broadly comparable task engagement, individuals with ASD rely on different PCC-centered neural mechanisms when integrating speaker-listener relationship information to infer communicative intentions.

item.title: Content-related motor cortical representation during attempted handwriting.
item.description:
Cell reports
Humans are superb at handwriting, and we can write in diverse ways, such as with a pen or with a fingertip. Remarkably, although different ways of writing involve divergent muscle activations, we can easily transfer our writing skill from one way to another without deliberate practice. Here, we investigated the neural substrates of this phenomenon by recording single-unit activity from the human motor cortex (MC) while a paralyzed participant attempted to write the same symbols under three effector conditions. Our results show that MC activity contains both content-related and effector-related information. Population analyses further indicate a content-related neural latent space shared across effector conditions. These findings suggest that a shared content-related subspace preserves writing content information across effector conditions and supports cross-effector decoding.

item.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain–computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices—signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set—into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time–frequency decomposition including the delta band (2–4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

item.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.

item.title: The language network responds stronger to connected than to unconnected sentences
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Purpose: Reliable functional mapping of the language network and preoperative assessment of language lateralization are essential for safe and effective craniotomy in patients with lesions in language‑eloquent brain regions, yet existing fMRI language paradigms are often time‑consuming and place substantial cognitive and economic demands on patients and diagnostic services. Methods: We therefore tested ecologically valid German stimulus sets designed to optimize measurement efficiency. Forty-three healthy participants (mean age = 38 years, range = 20 - 64; 24 women) were scanned on a 3T MRI while reading or listening to 4-, 8-, and 12-word sentences and pseudoword lists or texts, each followed by a decision task. Sentences were selected from German literary classics and text passages from general-interest science magazines and matched across conditions for lexical and structural properties. Results: Region‑of‑interest analyses in subject‑specific, functionally defined language‑sensitive regions showed robust activation of the left‑hemispheric language network across modalities. Within participants, texts elicited significantly larger effect sizes than sentences, and longer sentences generally produced stronger responses than shorter ones. Task manipulations expected to increase cognitive demand (short 4‑word sentences with frequent probes, coherent texts requiring deeper semantic integration) did not enhance responses in the domain‑general multiple demand network, indicating that executive‑control activity did not overshadow language‑selective activation, whereas substantial overlap between default mode and language‑sensitive regions in the left temporal lobe was consistent with relatively automatic processing of connected language. Conclusions: These findings indicate that ecologically valid sentence‑ and text‑based paradigms can provide efficient, language‑specific fMRI protocols for preoperative diagnostics and individualized presurgical planning in patients with lesions near language‑eloquent cortex.

item.title: Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing during Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.
item.description:
eNeuro
Language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation. Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels. In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components. These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.Significance statement Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages. Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level. These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

item.title: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain.
item.description:
Nature neuroscience
Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience. Multilingual neural network models offer a way to answer this question by representing linguistic content across languages in a shared space. Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Here we combined existing (12 languages across 4 language families) and newly collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data (9 languages across 4 families) to test encoding models predicting brain activity in the language network using representations from multilingual models. Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. This cross-lingual generalization extended across variation in language family, stimulus type and presentation modality. These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.

item.title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
Word meanings in language are contextualized by surrounding words. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism in transformer-based large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that structural composition in the brain arises from combining canonical (non-contextual) word representations with those of nearby words. We analysed single unit activity in the human hippocampus, a region involved in semantic and contextual processing, while n = 10 participants listened to podcasts. We found that hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause, using both ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Moreover, neural responses to specific words reflected both the lexical semantics of the word and a weighted sum of the embeddings of preceding words. The relative weighting of these contextualizing words correlated with LLM self-attention weights. These findings suggest that contextualization in the brain makes use of vectorial shifts that have a resemblance to attentional reweighting in LLMs, and highlight the role of the mesial temporal lobe within the broader language network.

item.title: Manipulating speech perception with amplitude-modulated kilohertz magnetic perturbation (AM-kTMP).
item.description:
Brain stimulation
Speech perception has been hypothesized to exploit neural activity that entrains to the rhythmic properties of the utterance. Perceptual sensitivity varies with the phase of oscillatory activity induced by speech, and with an external oscillatory perturbation induced by transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the temporal lobe. However, current non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) methods suffer from limitations that include peripheral nerve stimulation and hinder neural entrainment research. Here we used a new form of NIBS, kilohertz transcranial magnetic perturbation (kTMP), in which a low frequency perturbation is created by the amplitude modulation (AM) of a continuous high-frequency carrier signal (3.5 kHz). As a magnetic induction method, kTMP can produce much higher electrical fields at the cortical surface than tACS and reduces cutaneous co-stimulation. Human participants (n=40) listened to sequences of rhythmic speech while receiving kTMP with an AM component of 3.125 Hz. The phasic modulation of perceptual sensitivity was greater during AM-kTMP than during sham stimulation, consistent with the hypothesis that AM-kTMP entrained neural activity underlying speech perception. Participants' ratings of rhythmic sensations and other side effects did not differ between AM-kTMP and sham stimulation. Together with its reduced peripheral stimulation, our results highlight kTMP as a promising NIBS method for modulating frequency-specific brain dynamics in speech perception.

item.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

item.title: Neural competition predicts speech production advantages in congenital amusia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Mental health research has traditionally been deficit-focused, and cognitive advantages in mental conditions have almost always been documented retrospectively. Here we propose and test an a priori pathway for predicting such advantages from a condition's impaired neural basis, neural competition and brain-mind associations. Using congenital amusia (CA), a neurodevelopmental disorder with a well-defined deficit in right frontotemporal circuit (FTC), as a model, we predicted that interhemispheric competition would release the left homologue from inhibition, conferring advantages in speech production. Two independent studies, multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing, confirmed this prediction: MRI revealed right FTC impairment alongside competitive-like benefits of the left FTC in CA; and CA showed speech production advantages with intact episodic memory and constrained music learning. These findings provide the first empirical demonstration that cognitive advantages can be predicted in advance and then verified, offering a principled, mechanism-based alternative to the deficit-focused paradigm.

item.title: Discourse coherence in first-episode psychosis and depression: shared referential alterations and links to cortical hierarchy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Disrupted discourse coherence is documented in psychosis, but whether depression shows similar alterations, and how these relate to cortical hierarchical organization, remains unclear. This is the first study to examine conceptual and referential dimensions of coherence and their associations with cortical hierarchy across first-episode psychosis and depression. We analysed spontaneous speech from 85 German speakers (29 controls, 28 with first-episode psychosis, 28 with first-episode depression), of whom 80 underwent resting-state fMRI. Using large-model embeddings, automated coreference resolution, and graph-theoretical measures, we quantified conceptual relations (i.e., how ideas are linked) and referential relations (i.e., how entities are introduced and maintained), and related them to gradient dispersion between networks and within the semantic-associative network. Both clinical groups showed reduced referential continuity, and less small-world organization of conceptual content than controls, whereas differences in local semantic similarity depended on diagnosis and language model. Negative symptom severity was associated with altered conceptual and referential relations. Between-network gradient dispersion did not differ between groups. However, after controlling for diagnosis, individual variation in gradient organization was associated with distinct conceptual and referential relations. Visual-default mode network dispersion was associated with conceptual network organization, while somatomotor-default mode network dispersion was associated with local conceptual and referential coherence. Dispersion within the semantic-associative network was linked with topic reorganization. These findings identify reduced referential continuity as a shared, automatically measurable speech alteration across early psychosis and depression, linked to negative symptoms and cortical hierarchy, and support developing scalable speech-based markers for transdiagnostic assessment and differential diagnosis.

item.title: Mesial temporal function during language fMRI in pre-surgical epilepsy patients.
item.description:
Epilepsy research
Language fMRI paradigms may allow joint assessment of interconnected language and memory function before epilepsy surgery. We characterized activation of a core memory structure, mesial temporal lobe (MTL) during a language fMRI task. We investigated relationships between MTL activation and language and memory performance in individuals with epilepsy. We included 38 left focal epilepsy patients (18 adult, 20 pediatric), and 55 healthy controls (27 adult, 28 pediatric). Participants performed a clinically validated language fMRI task (Auditory Description Decision Task), language, and memory neuropsychological assessments. We computed lateralization index (LI) for bilateral Broca's and Wernicke's language areas and MTL memory regions of Interest (ROIs). We also investigated MTL activation magnitude across participant group (controls, patients), age group (adult, pediatric), MTL side (left, right), and region (anterior/posterior) with a mixed effects model. ANCOVAs assessed relationships between MTL LI or activation magnitude, and language and memory scores. All groups had left-lateralized MTL activation. We found greater MTL activation magnitude in adult than pediatric patients, and in pediatric controls than patients. Controls had greater anterior, and patients had greater posterior, activation magnitude. Left MTL lateralization was related to language, verbal, and visual memory function in children, and activation strength in left posterior MTL to verbal memory in adults. Our language fMRI task evoked left-lateralized language and MTL activation. Relationships between activation and neuropsychological tests suggest this activation is functionally relevant for evaluation of memory function. Our ADDT task may support both language and memory assessment before epilepsy surgery.

item.title: Speech and music organize neural activity differently over time in human superior temporal cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Speech and music engage overlapping auditory cortex. We asked whether they shape the timing of local activity in ways that regional response strength alone leaves unresolved. In intracranial recordings from 30 participants watching a film with alternating music and speech, 1-10-Hz activity in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) had higher sample entropy during music, indicating that similar short patterns were less likely to persist (mean paired difference = 0.02256, FDR q = 0.00753). The contrast persisted in comparisons of adjacent film blocks and was larger relative to surrogate signals matched for amplitude distribution and approximate power spectrum. Speech elicited higher STG high-frequency power in the intracranial subset and stronger bilateral STG BOLD responses in all 30 participants in the separately acquired fMRI recordings. Together, these findings show that the soundtrack category associated with stronger regional responses differs from the one associated with greater local temporal irregularity. The temporal organisation of local activity therefore adds a dimension to how shared auditory cortex responds to natural sounds.

item.title: The Dual Nature of Syntactic Node Count: Facilitating and Inhibiting Sentence Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Neurolinguistic research on syntactic processing has used Node Count, the number of syntactic nodes assumed to be built at each word, to investigate how structure-building effort affects brain activity. However, several recent studies cast doubt on the presumed link between Node Count and processing effort; they observe negative correlations between Node Count and reading times. These facilitatory effects raise an alternative hypothesis: rather than reflecting structure-building effort, Node Count may index structure-mediated predictability. To test this hypothesis, we first relate Node Count to an information-theoretic measure of contextual support, the pointwise mutual information (PMI) between a word and its context. We then evaluate the relationship between Node Count and reading times from three large-scale naturalistic English datasets. For these analyses, we derive Node Count under three grammar formalisms (phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar, and combinatory categorial grammar) and multiple parsing strategies. Variants whose count reflects integrative parsing steps correlate positively with PMI and show a dual behavioral profile: robust facilitation in immediate regions, consistent with structure-mediated predictability, and a delayed slowdown in spillover regions, most consistent with the cost of contextual semantic integration. The facilitatory effect explains reading-time variance beyond GPT-2 surprisal, indicating that Node Count has unique psycholinguistic value as an index of human prediction. These results highlight the role of structural representations in human language processing and underscore the need for a careful interpretation of the observed correlations between Node Count and brain activity in neurolinguistic studies.

item.title: Beyond the Group Average: Interindividual Variability in Neural Activity During Written Word Processing
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The processing of language and reading has been a subject of interest for neuropsychologists for many decades. Nevertheless, variability between subjects within the language network has received comparatively little attention. In this study, we employed a precision fMRI approach to examine between-subject variability in neural activity during single-word reading. In order to assess the similarity between subjects' activation patterns, two methods were utilised: Spearman's rank correlation and the Jaccard index. Following this, an exploratory correlation was performed between the similarity and subjects' characteristics. As part of the quantification of between-subject variance, the brain regions characterised by the most variance were identified using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC). The participants exhibited a moderate similarity in their activation patterns, which was correlated with their reading performance and psychopathological traits. Brain regions exhibiting notably high interindividual variability were predominantly located within or adjacent to the language network, suggesting variability in the precise location and extent of the language network among subjects. A comparison of the group-level activation map derived from the same sample revealed that it provided only a moderate representation of the individual maps. The findings underscore the significance of integrating group-level analyses with individual-centred methodologies to achieve more precise characterisation of the neural organisation of language and advance our understanding of the brain-behaviour relation.

item.title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke's area.
item.description:
Science (New York, N.Y.)
Wernicke's area in the posterior temporal lobe is classically defined by its role in speech comprehension, yet a paradox remains: Why does damage here also profoundly impair speech production? Using direct human brain recordings, cortical stimulation, and lesion analysis, we found that this region is not solely for perception. A discrete subzone within Wernicke's area, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), becomes active before speech, is causally necessary for speech production, and codes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulatory information. Its neural activity is distinct from the auditory-feedback responses nearby and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Thus, while Wernicke's area is a key part of auditory cortex, it contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation.

item.title: Quantity and quality of children's screen use and their neural and associated behavioral outcomes: A systematic review.
item.description:
Child development
The developmental impact of screen use on young children remains an active area of inquiry, with evidence of both risks and benefits depending on quantity and quality of exposure. This systematic review synthesized 23 neuroimaging studies of children aged 0-8 years, selected from 19,699 records identified across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and APA PsycINFO (2012-2025). Studies were included if they examined typically developing children, employed neuroimaging methods (EEG, fNIRS, or MRI), and assessed the effects of digital media exposure or intervention on brain and associated outcomes. Eight studies on quantity associated greater screen exposure with lower prefrontal activation, altered cortical activity, differences in white matter pathways, and lower myelination in language and cognitive regions. Fifteen studies on quality found that interactive and multimodal media, educational gamification, and caregiver co-use enhanced networks supporting language, perception, and socioemotional skills, whereas non-educational media showed null effects. Our paper argues that discussions on screen use should move beyond the sole focus on duration of screen-time to consider the dimensions of design, content, and context of media use and how they may shape developmental outcomes.

item.title: A "Basin of Attraction" Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article was to propose a theory of the neural basis of speech initiation that extends this idea to speech production and identifies a specific disruption that may underlie speech dysfluencies in stuttering. Method We advance a conceptual framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical (BGTC) circuit in initiating these trajectories. Results We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to steer the distributed speech motor network into the basin of attraction of the upcoming word's motor program. Stuttering arises when this process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms. Conclusions The basin of attraction framework provides a mechanistic description of the proximal neural processes responsible for stuttering events that can account for a wide range of behavioral and neurophysiological findings in stuttering. It also aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

item.title: Differential Impacts of Acoustic Challenge on Three Language-Related Event-Related Brain Potential Components During Speech Processing: Evidence From the N400, the P600, and a Late Frontal Response.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose When listening to acoustically challenging speech, listeners may strategically shift neural resources across multiple language-related cognitive processes in order to compensate for the additional demands. In the current study, we examined the impact of acoustic challenge (via speech-shaped background noise) on three language-related event-related brain potentials (ERPs): the N400 and two late positivities following the N400-a posterior P600 to syntactic violations and a late frontal effect sensitive to word expectancy. Method Young, normal-hearing adults (N = 48) listened in quiet and in noise (+3 dB SNR speech-shaped stationary noise) to contextually constraining sentences that ended in an expected word, an unexpected word, or a morphosyntactic violation of the expected word, while electroencephalography data were collected. Results Replicating prior work, we showed that an N400 expectancy effect was both reduced in amplitude and delayed in onset latency in noise. Providing novel insights into late ERP components, we found that a P600 syntax effect was reduced in amplitude by the presence of background noise. We additionally observed that the P600 response was only present for trials in which the listener successfully identified syntactic violations (irrespective of noise). In contrast to the reductions in the N400 and P600, the late frontal response was not reduced in noise. Conclusion Collectively, this suggests that, while semantic retrieval and syntactic integration may be impaired by acoustic challenge, young, normal-hearing listeners may still prioritize neural resources toward prediction-related processes to help compensate for increased perceptual demands.

item.title: Timing and meaning in spoken thought relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing (β = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.

item.title: Neural processing of linguistic speech features and their modulation by selective attention in users of hearing aids and cochlear implants
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding speech relies on the neural processing of acoustic and linguistic features, which can both be analyzed using Temporal Response Functions (TRFs). While both types of features have been the focus of numerous studies in typical-hearing individuals, much less is known about the neural processing of continuous speech for people with hearing loss, particularly how hearing-impaired listeners process word-level features in noisy environments, where they typically struggle. We recorded EEG from hearing aid (HA, n=29) and cochlear implant (CI, n=24) users, and an age-matched typical-hearing (TH) control group (n=29), while participants listened to audiobook segments in quiet and with a competing speaker, using their personal hearing devices (CI and HA). A hierarchical encoding framework incrementally added word onset, word frequency, and word surprisal as predictors of the EEG signal. Attentional modulation was assessed by comparing encoding scores for attended versus ignored speech. All three groups showed clear neural responses to word onset, frequency, and surprisal for speech in quiet. Surprisal tracking emerged at 400 ms in TH participants, 500 ms in HA users, and 600 ms in CI users, weakest in the CI group. All three groups exhibited attentional modulation of surprisal tracking. Word frequency yielded significant encoding gains in quiet only for TH and HI listeners, not CI users. We show for the first time that CI users exhibit significant, attention-modulated neural responses to word surprisal. More broadly, surprisal tracking was present across all hearing-impaired groups but weakest in CI users, the cohort with the greatest difficulty understanding speech in noise.

item.title: Neural sensitivity to musical rhythm is associated with the temporal dynamics of statistical learning in speech
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Statistical learning enables the extraction of structure from the environment, including word units from continuous speech. Yet inter-individual variability suggests contributions from other, potentially broader domain-general mechanisms. Here, we investigated whether individual differences in music rhythm processing are associated with the dynamics of statistical learning during speech segmentation, potentially reflecting shared sensitivity to temporal regularities across music and language. Adults were exposed to structured and random artificial speech streams while neural tracking at syllable and word rate frequencies was tracked over time using EEG to characterize the emergence of word representations. In addition, participants’ abilities to process rhythm in musical materials were assessed using behavioral and neural (EEG) measures. Neural measurements revealed robust tracking at the syllabic level in both structured and random streams, whereas word-level tracking emerged over exposure only in the structured stream condition. Importantly, individual differences in neural synchronization to musical rhythms were associated with the temporal dynamics of word extraction. These results suggest that individual differences in the ability to process temporal regularities in musical material are related to the efficiency with which statistical regularities are extracted from sequential language material. More broadly, the findings provide evidence for domain-general mechanisms supporting sensitivity to temporal structure regularities across auditory domains.

item.title: Cross-domain encoding models reveal shared and domain-specific neural representations across language and mathematics.
item.description:
Science advances
Whether language and mathematics rely on shared or distinct neural representations remains unresolved in cognitive neuroscience. Here, we combined latent features from a large language model with functional magnetic resonance imaging encoding models to test cross-domain generalization in 32 participants performing sentence comprehension and calculation tasks. Cross-domain prediction identified cortical regions showing partially shared representations, most consistently in the left area 55b, while control analyses suggested that these effects could not be fully explained by low-level visual or task-general factors. Domain-specificity contrasts revealed stronger language-related prediction in the left superior temporal sulcus and angular gyrus and math-related prediction in the left precentral sulcus and bilateral intraparietal sulci. Model-weight analyses revealed distinct weight profiles associated with shared and domain-specific prediction patterns. Cross-domain regions also exhibited task-dependent functional coupling with language- and math-related networks. Together, these findings suggest that language and mathematics involve partially shared neural representations alongside domain-specific cortical organization, helping reconcile previous contrasting views on their neural basis.

item.title: Auditory cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulations is sufficient to support perceptual categorization of speech and music.
item.description:
Science advances
Auditory processing is typically described as hierarchical, culminating in neural representation of abstract categories. However, it remains unclear whether category-selective responses in auditory cortex require representational mechanisms beyond the coding of acoustic features or whether the acoustic representations already available in the auditory cortex are sufficient to account for categorization. Here, we test whether cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulation (STM) features is sufficient to support speech-music categorization by combining human intracranial recordings with continuous behavioral judgments of a naturalistic soundtrack in which speech and music occur both separately and simultaneously. We show that temporal and spectral modulation patterns largely characterize speech and music, respectively, and that cortical auditory regions robustly track these features over time, with distinct oscillatory frequency bands preferentially encoding temporal and spectral modulations. Critically, cortical representations of STMs predicted perceptual categorical judgments gathered in an independent sample. Last, speech- and music-related STM representations showed stronger tracking of category-specific acoustical features in left versus right cortical auditory regions, respectively. These findings indicate that the efficient neural coding of acoustical features provides a sufficient basis for the categorical distinction between speech and music and that the temporal and spectral components of this representation are implemented through distinct oscillatory mechanisms.

item.title: An electrophysiological investigation of inhibitory control in children with dyslexia and the role of comorbid ADHD symptoms: a pilot randomized intervention study.
item.description:
Child neuropsychology : a journal on normal and abnormal development in childhood and adolescence
Neurobiological research indicates that atypical functioning within left-hemisphere parietal and temporal regions is associated with word-processing difficulties in children with dyslexia. This study used event-related potentials (ERPs) to examine the neural correlates of inhibitory control in children with dyslexia, the effects of computerized inhibition training, and the influence of ADHD symptoms. This pilot study employed a randomized, double-blind, dosage-controlled intervention design. Participants were 62 children aged 10-12 years, including 37 children with dyslexia and 25 typically-developing controls (TDCs). Intervention analyses included 34 children with dyslexia assigned to high (n = 18) or low-dose (n = 16) training. Behavioral performance, electrophysiological responses during a Go/No-Go task, and ADHD symptoms were assessed. Independent samples t-tests showed that children with dyslexia exhibited significantly slower reaction times than TDCs during the picture Go/No-Go task. Children with dyslexia also demonstrated reduced left-lateralized N2 and P3 amplitudes over fronto-central and fronto-temporal regions relative to TDCs at baseline. ADHD inattentive symptoms were significantly associated with slower reaction times at baseline. Mixed-factorial ANOVAs revealed significant reductions in reaction times across both training groups, together with pre- to post-intervention changes in several N2 and P3 indices. These findings suggest that children with dyslexia exhibit altered neural correlates of inhibitory control despite relatively modest behavioral differences and highlight the importance of considering ADHD symptomatology when investigating executive functioning in dyslexia.

item.title: The level of cortical thickening in executive functions and audiovisual integration regions predicts reading comprehension via reading fluency in musically experienced children.
item.description:
Brain research
Proficient reading fluency, which is critical for intact reading comprehension, is related to efficient audio-visual integration and to executive functions (EF). Interestingly, musical training has been associated with better audio-visual integration, EF, and reading abilities. However, the direct relationship, cognitively and neurobiologically, between these components remains ambiguous. Here, we examined the neurobiological correlates of the predictive role of EF and audio-visual integration on reading comprehension through fluency in children with and without music experience using cortical thickness (CT) measures. A high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical scan was acquired from 8- to 12-year-old children with and without music experience. CT within EF (anterior cingulate cortex) and audio-visual (insula) brain regions was compared between groups. A moderated mediation analysis was conducted with anterior cingulate cortex CT as the predictor variable, reading comprehension as the outcome variable, reading fluency as the mediator, and music experience as the moderator, with age and sex as covariates. Musically inexperienced children demonstrated lower reading fluency, comprehension, and EF abilities compared to experienced children. In experienced children, CT in the anterior cingulate gyrus predicted comprehension via an indirect pathway mediated by fluency (B = 21.63, BootSE = 9.11, 95 % CI [4.56, 40.85]); in inexperienced children, neither the direct nor indirect pathways significantly predicted comprehension (B = 11.53, BootSE = 8.64, 95 % CI [-6.54, 28.80]). The Index of Moderated Mediation was not significant (IMM = - 10.10, BootSE = 11.79, 95 % CI [-34.92, 12.21]); thus, there was no statistical evidence that the indirect effect differed between the groups. Results suggest that musical experience is associated with differences in neural circuits linked to EF and audiovisual integration, which in turn relate to reading fluency and comprehension.

item.title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

item.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

item.title: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
ABSTRACT Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face– and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision– and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

item.title: Immature Valence Recognition of Emotional Speech in Cochlear Implant Users: Evidence From Event-Related Potentials and Neural Oscillations.
item.description:
Ear and hearing
Objectives Rapid emotional perception in speech is crucial to efficient social communication. Cochlear implant (CI) users, constrained by device limitations in transmitting spectro-temporal detail, rely more on semantic than prosodic cues for emotional processing of spoken language. This study investigated whether CI users can rapidly recognize emotional valence based on semantic cues before full semantic comprehension when prosodic information is minimized. Design Chinese monosyllables with negative or positive valence were presented with neutral prosody using an oddball paradigm. Event-related potentials and neural oscillations were recorded in CI users and normal-hearing (NH) listeners. Results Emotional syllables evoked an N400, indicative of semantic processing, in NH listeners. Crucially, NH listeners showed an earlier mismatch negativity (MMN) for negative syllable deviants, reflecting rapid categorical perception of emotional valence. However, the N400 for positive deviants and the MMN were absent in CI users. Furthermore, compared with NH listeners, CI users showed weaker theta-band and alpha-band event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs) and inter-trial coherences and a greater beta-band ERSP. A lower beta-band ERSP was correlated with greater N400 and late negative component in NH listeners. Personality scores for extraversion and agreeableness correlated with the amplitudes of the MMN and N400 components, respectively. Conclusions The findings portray the dynamics of emotional speech processing and demonstrate that rapid recognition of emotional valence expressed by lexical meaning occurs before complete semantic processing in the NH brain. Theta activity may be associated with early emotional valence recognition, and beta activity corresponds to higher-level semantic and emotional processing. However, these two processes are immature in CI users, as evidenced by absent event-related potentials and altered neural oscillations. Personality traits may modulate emotional sensitivity, further affecting the efficiency of emotional speech processing.

item.title: Active L2 immersion is associated with glymphatic-related MRI markers in healthy young adults: A cross-sectional multimodal study.
item.description:
Neuroimage. Reports
Background The brain's glymphatic system plays a vital role in maintaining neural health. However, little is known about whether second language (L2) immersion is associated with glymphatic function. Methods 50 high-proficiency L2 English speakers (mean age: 32.6 years; 78% female) underwent multimodal MRI. Three glymphatic-related markers were derived: BOLD-CSF coupling strength (fMRI), choroid plexus (ChP) ratio (structural MRI), and DTI-ALPS index (diffusion MRI). We examined their associations with L2 immersion duration and age of acquisition (AOA), and active language-use context, controlling for age, education, and sex. Results Longer L2 immersion duration was associated with stronger BOLD-CSF coupling (r = -.316, q = .029; two-tailed q = .059) and smaller ChP ratios (r = -.386, q = .016). An exploratory mediation analysis indicated an indirect association with the ALPS index through ChP ratio and BOLD-CSF coupling. AOA moderated the immersion-coupling association, significant among earlier learners (B = -.134, p < .001) but not later learners. AOA did not moderate the ChP association and ALPS index. Only active L2 use within immersive environments was associated with the markers, whereas passive immersion and non-immersive active use were not. Conclusions L2 immersion duration is associated directly and indirectly with MRI-derived glymphatic-related markers in healthy adults. These findings extend research on bilingualism and brain health to glymphatic-related physiology and motivate longitudinal tests of whether this association contributes to cognitive reserve.

item.title: Multidimensional psycholinguistic difficulty in Cantonese picture naming: Behavioral, neural, and effective connectivity evidence.
item.description:
Brain and language
Picture naming is a useful paradigm for studying spoken word production because it requires the transformation of visual object input into a lexical response through coordinated conceptual and lexical processes. This study examined whether inherent psycholinguistic difficulty in picture naming is multidimensional or unitary. Thirty-eight healthy native Cantonese speakers performed an overt object picture-naming task during fMRI. Four psycholinguistic variables were modeled: conceptual familiarity, average neighborhood distance (AND), naming disagreement, and lexical frequency. Mixed-effects models showed that higher conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency facilitated naming, whereas higher AND increased both errors and response times; naming disagreement increased errors but did not significantly affect response times. Importantly, we observed a significant interaction between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency on response times, indicating the facilitative effect of frequency was modulated by familiarity. For errors, significant interactions were found between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency, as well as between AND and lexical frequency, and between AND and naming disagreement, revealing complex joint influences on naming accuracy. Whole-brain analyses revealed dissociable neural effects across variables. Conjunction analysis showed that lower conceptual familiarity and higher AND converged in bilateral lateral occipital and ventral occipitotemporal regions, with extension into the left posterior temporal cortex, suggesting shared sensitivity to semantic-level difficulty. In contrast, naming disagreement and lexical frequency did not show significant lexical-level overlap. Effective connectivity analyses further identified a stable directed ROI architecture during naming. Together, the findings support a multidimensional account of picture-naming difficulty in which semantic- and lexical-related item properties impose partially distinct but interacting constraints on spoken word production.

item.title: Speech and Language Abnormalities in Putative Brain-First Versus Body-First Parkinson's Disease.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
Background The α-synuclein origin model proposes brain-first and body-first Parkinson's disease (PD) subtypes, with speech potentially revealing their distinct neurodegenerative patterns. Objective We aimed to analyze the possible speech and language differences between untreated PD patients with premotor (putative body-first) and without (putative brain-first) rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Methods Speech samples of reading passages and monologues were automatically analyzed using acoustic and linguistic features. Results We enrolled 23 body-first and 35 brain-first de novo PD patients compared with 35 healthy controls. Brain-first patients showed greater speech impairment severity compared with body-first patients (P = 0.002) and controls (P < 0.001), whereas body-first patients showed greater language impairment severity compared with brain-first patients (P < 0.001) and controls (P < 0.001). Conclusions Putative brain-first subtype had more motor speech abnormalities whereas body-first subtype manifested greater language impairment. Thes finding is consistent with motor-dominant nigrostriatal involvement in brain-first and broader non-motor/cognitive involvement in body-first PD. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

item.title: Neurophysiological evidence for rapid semantic integration via fast mapping.
item.description:
Cognitive, affective & behavioral neuroscience
Theories of declarative memory consolidation hold that novel associative information is integrated into cortical semantic networks slowly and with hippocampal support. However, an encoding paradigm called fast mapping (FM) has been proposed to permit rapid cortical integration of novel item-label associations, particularly when the novel item shares substantial visual-semantic features with a simultaneously presented known concept. We tested whether associations encoded through FM immediately engage semantic memory networks, indexed by the N400 event-related potential. In contrast to behavioral semantic priming tasks, in which semantic relatedness and response congruency may be confounded, the present EEG study provides a more process-specific test of rapid semantic integration. Sixty participants encoded pairs of a novel item and an unfamiliar label under two conditions, differing with respect to the visual-semantic overlap between the novel item and a simultaneously presented known item. In a subsequent semantic priming task, the novel labels served as primes for semantically related versus unrelated targets. While behavioral results did not reveal a significant priming effect, EEG data indicated an N400 priming effect in the high-overlap FM condition, characterized by reduced N400 amplitudes for related compared with unrelated targets over a parietal electrode cluster. Crucially, the N400 effect was significantly larger after high-overlap FM than after low-overlap FM encoding, indicating that high feature overlap enhances rapid semantic integration already minutes after learning. These findings provide the first neurophysiological evidence that high-overlap FM enables rapid semantic integration.

item.title: Persistent neuroimmune alterations in children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected at age 6-7 years: Associations with language development in a South African birth cohort.
item.description:
Brain, behavior, and immunity
Background Children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected (HEU) are at increased risk of neurodevelopmental delays, yet neuroimmune pathways linking perinatal HIV exposure to school readiness remain unclear. Methods In the Drakenstein Child Health Study, 267 children (93 HEU, 174 HIV-unexposed [HU]) underwent magnetic resonance spectroscopy in midline parietal grey and left parietal white matter regions at 6-7 years. Peripheral blood serum immune markers were measured in pregnancy and in children at 6 weeks, 2, 3, and 5 years. Linear mixed-effects models characterised child immune trajectories and linear regressions tested associations with creatine-referenced neurometabolite ratios and school readiness scores. Results Mothers living with HIV had higher sCD14 and lower MMP-9, NGAL, and GM-CSF than mothers without HIV (p < 0.05). Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with altered trajectories of child sCD14, GM-CSF, IL-1β, IL-5, IL-10, and YKL-40. At 6-7 years, children who were HEU had lower parietal grey matter glutamate ratios and lower left parietal white matter choline ratios. By school entry, more frequent associations between child immune markers and neurometabolites were observed, with IL-8 emerging as a recurrent correlate across developmental stages. Children who were HEU had lower language scores than HU peers. Left parietal white matter choline ratios were positively associated with language and overall school readiness in HU children, but not HEU. Conclusions Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with alterations in immune development, neurometabolites reflecting both white matter maturation and neuronal health, and school readiness. Our findings highlight potential neuroimmune alterations contributing to neurodevelopmental risks in children who are HEU. A single explanatory pathway was not identified, supporting the need for longitudinal studies of neuroimmune, clinical, and environmental contributors to developmental vulnerability in this population.

item.title: Brain2voice 2.0: High-performance voice synthesis brain-computer interface.
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising solution to speech loss due to neurological injury by decoding intended speech directly from brain activity. While recent BCIs have restored high-accuracy text-based communication, they fail to provide instantaneous voice output essential for the natural flow of conversation. Brain-to-voice BCIs address this gap by decoding voice directly from neural signals. However, even the state-of-the-art (SOTA) BCI-synthesized voice is not yet intelligible enough for real-world adoption. We introduce brain2voice 2.0, a new multimodal Transformer-based BCI decoder architecture capable of synthesizing highly intelligible voice from intracortical neural signals in real-time. Brain2voice 2.0 is trained on continuous and custom-tokenized acoustic targets and phoneme targets, leveraging their complementary speech information. We use self-supervised and adversarial training objectives that enhance acoustic feature quality and improve synthesis intelligibility. At each 10 ms timestep, the model causally outputs continuous and tokenized acoustic features for real-time voice synthesis as well as time-aligned phoneme predictions (raw phoneme error rate: 7%, comparable to the latest brain-to-text models). We evaluated this new approach on our prior intracortical brain-to-voice benchmark dataset (Wairagkar et al. 2025). Naive human listeners transcribed brain2voice 2.0 synthesized voice with a word error rate of 5.24%-an 8× improvement in intelligibility over previous SOTA results (43.75%). Brain2voice 2.0 demonstrates that highly intelligible real-time voice synthesis from neural signals is achievable, for the first time crossing the intelligibility threshold necessary for clinically viable brain-to-voice BCIs for people with paralysis.

item.title: Central Motor Injury as Interlayer Decoupling: An Evolutionary Information Layering Framework for Neurorehabilitation
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Central motor injury is often framed as a loss of cortical command, leading rehabilitation to prioritize early cortical reactivation and active task practice. This framing captures an important part of motor impairment but leaves a second problem under-specified: how injury disrupts communication among mechanical, spinal-peripheral, and supraspinal coordination layers. The Evolutionary Information Layering (EIL) framework proposes that biological coordination develops through the retention, specialization, and integration of ancestral regulatory systems rather than through their replacement. Applying EIL to neurorehabilitation, this article conceptualizes severe central motor injury as interlayer decoupling, defined here as a loss of phase-, context-, and task-appropriate conditional influence among functional layers. Three interacting disturbances are proposed: reduced reliability of descending commands, maladaptive gain from residual descending activity, and preserved but insufficiently engaged lower-layer mechanical and spinal coordination. Rehabilitation can therefore be organized as layer reweighting rather than as competition between cortical and spinal mechanisms. The therapeutic sequence is to titrate premature higher-layer demand, re-engage structured lower-layer information, and progressively reintegrate higher-level predictive control. The framework generates testable predictions concerning phase-dependent spinal modulation, proximal coordination, and task-specific cortical engagement. It also provides a theoretical basis for lower-layer-informed rehabilitation protocols without claiming that spinal circuits replace cortical function. Because most indirect evidence comes from stroke and human locomotor or spinal cord studies, application to traumatic brain injury and other central nervous system disorders should remain diagnosis-dependent.

item.title: Children with developmental language disorder show selective impairments in low-frequency neural tracking of speech.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Neural tracking of slow temporal modulations in speech supports extraction of the prosodic and syllabic structure thought to be critical for language acquisition by Temporal Sampling (TS) theory, yet whether these automatic cortical tracking mechanisms are altered in children with developmental language disorder (DLD) remains unclear. We recorded MEG while children with and without DLD listened to a story, and quantified source-level lagged speech-brain coherence and frequency-specific cortical functional connectivity across bilateral cortical regions. As expected a priori by TS theory, children with DLD showed significantly reduced coherence in the 0.9-2.5 Hz range associated with prosodic information in the story, spanning bilateral auditory and speech-related cortex. The strongest regional group differences were in left supramarginal gyrus (p < 0.001) and right inferior frontal gyrus (p = 0.001). In the 2.5-5 Hz range, linked to syllabic-rate modulations in the story, children with DLD showed reduced coherence in right temporal regions (all p < 0.02). Stronger low-frequency speech-brain coherence was associated with better language performance, indicating that individual differences in cortical speech tracking were behaviourally meaningful. No reliable differences were observed at higher modulation rates (5-9 Hz or 12-40 Hz). Exploratory functional connectivity analyses did not reveal network-level group differences that were robust across ROI time-series extraction methods. These findings indicate that atypical low-frequency neural tracking of speech is functionally relevant to language outcomes in DLD.
